strengths: The paper targets a well-motivated practical problem (single-step, low-latency generative policies for robot manipulation) and builds incrementally but sensibly on a recent and relevant baseline (MP1/MeanFlow).
The proposed Cosine/Directional Alignment loss is simple, lightweight, and easy to integrate into existing MeanFlow-based training pipelines without adding network depth or parameters.

Empirical results on a fairly large task suite (37 tasks across Adroit and Meta-World, 3 seeds) show consistent and, on harder task subsets (Medium/Hard/Very-Hard Meta-World), sizeable improvements over MP1 and FlowPolicy while retaining single-step (NFE=1) inference speed.
The ablation study (Table 2) isolates the contribution of the dispersive loss, the cosine loss, and the DDE approximation, giving some insight into which component drives the improvement.
The paper is reasonably well organized with a clear related-work positioning relative to diffusion-based, flow-based, and MeanFlow-based policies.
weaknesses: The abstract explicitly claims OMP addresses MP1's 'lack of few-shot generalization,' but no experiment varies the number of demonstrations or otherwise directly measures few-shot generalization; the only evidence offered is standard success-rate comparisons under a fixed 10-demo setting, so this central claim is unsupported by the experiments provided.

The theoretical motivation (Section 4.2) treats generic high-dimensional MSE regression gradient starvation as a novel finding, but the argument is elementary vector calculus (Law of Cosines) and does not rigorously connect to the specific structure of the MeanFlow identity (Eq. 4) that the model actually optimizes; the paper aligns predictions with v0 = zT − z0 (the full 0-to-1 displacement) even though training samples arbitrary sub-intervals [r,t], and the assumption that the local average velocity over [r,t] should point in the same direction as the global displacement is not justified or discussed, especially for curved/multimodal trajectories.

The claimed reduction in GPU memory usage from replacing JVP with the Differential Derivation Equation (DDE) is never quantified (no memory numbers, no wall-clock comparison); only a success-rate ablation is reported, which actually shows a performance drop, making the practical value of this contribution unclear.

Equation (11), which defines the DDE approximation, contains an apparent typo/inconsistency in the argument ordering of the two terms in the numerator, undermining confidence in the correctness of the reported method.

Key hyperparameters (λ_Disp, λ_cos, the perturbation constant ϵ in DDE, and cosine-loss temperature) are never specified with concrete values, and no code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility.

Improvements over MP1 are modest and, for several task categories, fall within or close to overlapping standard deviations (e.g., Hard tasks: 62.5±3.1 vs. 58.1±5.0), raising questions about statistical significance given only 3 random seeds.

DM1, described in the related work as the most closely related concurrent method (also using MeanFlow + dispersive regularization for one-step manipulation), is not included in the main quantitative comparison table, leaving an important direct baseline comparison missing.
The manuscript contains multiple typographical and formatting issues (e.g., 'twnety-one', inconsistent notation in Eq. 11, unclear task splits/counts) that detract from polish and clarity.

strengths: The paper tackles a practical problem (single-step generative policies for real-time robot manipulation) and builds on a timely framework (MeanFlow).

Empirical results show consistent gains over MP1 and FlowPolicy, particularly on the harder subsets of Meta-World (Medium/Hard/Very Hard), which is a meaningful practical finding if the comparisons are fair.

The idea of a lightweight cosine-similarity term to decouple directional learning from magnitude learning is intuitive and cheap to implement, and the paper reports an ablation isolating its contribution.
The paper is accompanied by reasonably detailed implementation hyperparameters, which aids partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central theoretical motivation in Sec 4.2 appears conceptually flawed: v0 is defined as zT − z0, i.e., the vector from a standard Gaussian noise sample to the clean action, not the robot's instantaneous task-space velocity. There is no justification for why ||v0|| would shrink for 'high-precision' tasks like Peg Insert, since zT is always drawn from N(0,I) regardless of task precision; the gradient-starvation argument therefore conflates the flow's noise-to-action vector with physical action velocity, undermining the claimed root cause and the necessity of the proposed Cosine Loss.

The derivation in Sec 4.2 (Law-of-Cosines decomposition of MSE) is a generic, well-known property of vector regression and is not specific to MeanFlow or robotics; presenting it as a key theoretical contribution overstates its novelty.

Equation 11 (the DDE finite-difference approximation of the JVP) contains an inconsistent/erroneous expression (the denominator term lists variables as 'zt, t, ϵ, r' instead of 'zt, t, r', and the perturbed term only perturbs t but not r despite the identity depending on (t-r)); this suggests insufficient care in the technical exposition and makes the method hard to reproduce exactly as written.

DM1, explicitly described in Related Work as 'closely related' and also using MeanFlow with dispersive regularization for one-step manipulation, is omitted from the main quantitative comparison (Table 1) and ablations, despite being the most direct competitor; its absence is a significant gap that undermines the significance claims.

The abstract and intro emphasize 'few-shot generalization' as a key benefit, but no experiment directly varies the number of demonstrations or evaluates generalization to unseen object/task variations; all results use a fixed 10 demonstrations per task under the standard training protocol, so the few-shot claim is not directly substantiated.

The overall improvement over the strongest baseline (MP1) is modest (3.4% average), and the paper itself acknowledges this, pivoting the narrative to subset results (Medium/Hard/Very Hard) after the fact; this selective emphasis weakens confidence in the robustness and generality of the claimed gains.

In the ablation (Table 2), replacing JVP with DDE increases performance on the Pen task (58→64) with no explanation, which is inconsistent with the paper's narrative that DDE is strictly an approximation trade-off; this anomaly is not discussed and raises questions about the reliability/variance of the reported numbers (only 3 seeds).

No code or model release is mentioned, and critical implementation details (e.g., exact architecture, value of ε in DDE, λ weighting schedule for Lcos/LDisp) are not specified, limiting reproducibility.
Presentation contains multiple minor but indicative errors (e.g., 'twnety-one' instead of 'twenty-one', inconsistent notation in Eq. 11), suggesting the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

The paper relies heavily on very recent (2025, including some seemingly unpublished arXiv) baselines and discussion (e.g., DM1, World4RL, TR-DRL, CLAP) without deeper critical engagement, and the writing in places reads as a loosely connected list of related works rather than a focused comparison that clarifies OMP's unique positioning.

strengths: Strong empirical results: OMP improves average success rate over the direct MeanFlow robotics baseline (MP1) by 3.4% and over FlowPolicy by 10.7% across 37 Adroit/Meta-World tasks, with particularly large gains on Medium/Hard/Very-Hard Meta-World tasks (4.4-10.6% improvement), which is where the paper's motivating failure mode (gradient starvation for small target velocities) should matter most.

Reasonably clear and intuitive theoretical motivation: the Law-of-Cosines decomposition of MSE gradient (Eq. 6-7) gives a plausible mechanistic explanation for why standard MeanFlow training underweights directional accuracy when target velocity magnitude is small, which is used to motivate the Cosine Loss.

The ablation study (Table 2) isolates the contribution of the Dispersive Loss, the Cosine Loss, and the DDE approximation, showing that removing directional alignment causes the largest performance drop, lending some support to the central claim.
Good coverage of baselines and tasks (DP, AdaFlow, CP, DP3, Simple DP3, FlowPolicy, MP1 across 37 tasks, 3 seeds), and the paper reports standard deviations, which aids assessment of robustness.
Training stability/convergence curves (Figure 4) provide some additional qualitative evidence of smoother optimization with the proposed loss.
weaknesses: Central claim/evidence mismatch: the abstract and introduction explicitly attribute MP1's lack of few-shot generalization to 'fixed temperature hyperparameters in its Dispersive Loss,' but the Method section never modifies or adapts this temperature hyperparameter — the actual contributions (Cosine Loss and DDE) do not address this stated problem at all. This is a significant inconsistency between the paper's motivating claim and its technical contribution.

No experiments vary the number of demonstrations (fixed at 10 per task throughout), so the claimed 'few-shot generalization' improvement is never directly tested; all evidence is from a single fixed low-data regime rather than a sweep demonstrating generalization as a function of shot count.

The DDE approximation (Eq. 11) appears to only perturb the time argument t while holding z_t fixed, which does not correctly approximate the total derivative d/dt u(z_t,r,t) required by the MeanFlow Identity (which also depends on dz/dt = v). The equation as written also contains a notational inconsistency ('uθ(zt, t, ϵ, r|c)' in the second term), making it unclear exactly what is computed; this undermines confidence in the technical soundness of one of the two core contributions.

Despite claiming the DDE 'significantly reduces GPU memory consumption,' no memory measurements (e.g., peak GPU memory, memory vs. task complexity) are reported anywhere in the paper — only FPS/latency trade-offs are shown in Figure 1. This leaves the paper's second major contribution empirically unverified.

DM1 (Zou et al., 2025), a closely related and seemingly concurrent MeanFlow + dispersive-regularization robotic policy, is discussed in Related Work and explicitly contrasted with OMP's design, but is never included as an empirical baseline in Table 1, leaving the comparative claim of superiority over DM1 unsubstantiated.

The ablated baseline '-Ldis-Lcos' (which should approximate vanilla MeanFlow/MP1) produces notably different numbers from the actual MP1 row in Table 1 (e.g., Door 66±3 vs 69±2, Pen 48±4 vs 58±5), suggesting discrepancies in re-implementation that are not explained, raising questions about the fairness/consistency of baseline reproduction.
Key hyperparameters (λ_Disp, λ_cos, the finite-difference perturbation ϵ) are not reported in the experimental setup, and no code/checkpoint release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility.

The geometric motivation in Section 4.2, while intuitively presented, is a fairly standard observation about MSE regression gradients and does not constitute a particularly novel theoretical contribution; similarly the Cosine Loss itself is a well-known technique (direction-magnitude decoupling) applied in a new context rather than a fundamentally new idea.

Minor presentation issues (e.g., 'twnety-one' typo, duplicated/garbled subsection heading in Section 4 intro, Equation 11 notation) suggest the manuscript would benefit from a careful proofreading pass.

strengths: The paper identifies and motivates a concrete, underexplored problem when applying the MeanFlow paradigm to robotic manipulation: spectral bias (low-pass filtering behavior of the averaging operator), gradient starvation in low-velocity/high-precision regimes, and the memory overhead of nested JVP computations. These are illustrated with both toy synthetic experiments (Fig. 2) and closed-form derivations (Appendix B).

The proposed fix (directional alignment via cosine-similarity loss decoupled from magnitude, plus a finite-difference Differential Derivation Equation approximating the JVP) is simple, lightweight, and directly targets the diagnosed failure modes, making the contribution interpretable and easy to implement.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 37 simulated tasks (Adroit + Meta-World, stratified by difficulty) and 3 real-world manipulation tasks, with multiple seeds, ablations isolating the dispersive loss and directional alignment terms, and a sensitivity study over action-chunk horizons (Appendix E) and a JVP-vs-DDE memory/accuracy trade-off analysis (Table 3).

OMP shows consistent, and on harder task subsets (Meta-World Medium/Hard/Very Hard, real-world Slip Ring) substantial, improvements over strong recent baselines (MP1, FlowPolicy, DP3) while retaining single-step (NFE=1) inference, and exhibits qualitatively more stable training curves (Fig. 5) than baselines.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis, while presented with formal notation (Theorem B.1, gradient decompositions), rests on simplified linear/toy assumptions (e.g., treating trajectories as stationary stochastic processes, continuous-time gradient flow rather than the Adam optimizer actually used) and is validated only on small synthetic examples (sum-of-sines, 2D toy vectors); it is not clearly established that these idealized derivations transfer to the nonlinear, high-dimensional point-cloud policy networks used in the main experiments.

The core methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: a cosine-similarity alignment loss is a well-known technique, the dispersive loss is adopted from prior work (Geng et al., 2025a), and the finite-difference derivative approximation is explicitly motivated by Wang et al. (2025c). The main new element is the specific combination for MeanFlow policies, a modest algorithmic contribution relative to the strong theoretical framing in the paper.

Improvements over the strongest baseline (MP1) are fairly small in aggregate (82.3% vs 78.9%, a 3.4-point gain) and most of the gain is concentrated in a subset of harder tasks; on easy tasks performance is near-saturated, and the ablation shows directional alignment alone contributes only ~4 points, tempering claims that this mechanism is a 'critical' fix.

The DDE approximation introduces a free hyperparameter (perturbation constant epsilon) whose selection, stability, and sensitivity are not analyzed, despite this component being central to the claimed memory-efficiency contribution.

Real-world evaluation is based on only 20 trials per task across 3 tasks with no reported variance/confidence intervals, and neither simulated nor real-world results include formal statistical significance testing across seeds/trials, weakening confidence in the reported margins.

The abstract/claims mention improvements in 'trajectory accuracy,' but no explicit trajectory-accuracy metric (e.g., trajectory MSE, DTW) is reported in the main results — only success rate — creating a mismatch between stated contributions and presented evidence.

Presentation has some inconsistencies (e.g., unclear which OMP variant, JVP or DDE, corresponds to 'Ours' in Figure 1; minor grammatical issues) and reproducibility relies on supplementary material/code that is not independently verifiable in the review process.

strengths: The paper provides a reasonably clear theoretical narrative connecting MeanFlow's integral formulation to a spectral low-pass filtering effect (Theorem B.1) and to a 'gradient starvation' phenomenon in low-velocity/high-precision regimes (Sec 4.2.2, App B.2), giving an interpretable motivation for the proposed fixes.

Broad empirical evaluation across 37 simulated tasks (Adroit + Meta-World, split into easy/medium/hard/very-hard) plus 3 real-world manipulation tasks, with multiple strong recent baselines (DP, DP3, AdaFlow, CP, FlowPolicy, MP1).

Ablation study (Table 1) and a sensitivity analysis over action-chunk horizons (Table 5, App E.1) isolate the contributions of the dispersive loss, directional-alignment loss, and the JVP-vs-DDE approximation, which is good practice for attributing gains to specific design choices.

The memory-efficiency argument for replacing the exact JVP with a finite-difference DDE is empirically substantiated with concrete GPU memory measurements (Table 3), showing a practically meaningful reduction (e.g., ~7.5GB savings on a larger point-cloud task).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is relatively incremental: a cosine-similarity 'directional alignment' auxiliary loss term and a standard central finite-difference approximation of a Jacobian-vector product (explicitly 'motivated by' prior work, Wang et al. 2025c). Neither technique is conceptually new to the broader deep learning/flow-matching literature, limiting originality.

The headline theoretical result (Theorem B.1) essentially restates that time-averaging acts as an integrator/low-pass filter in the frequency domain—a well-known signal-processing fact—rather than a deep, robotics-specific theoretical insight; its practical implications for actual policy training (beyond the synthetic sine-wave toy experiment in App C.1) are not rigorously connected to the real benchmark results.

The paper explicitly identifies DM1 (Zou et al., 2025) as one of the two 'most relevant predecessors' to this work (both addressing the same directional-drift issue in MeanFlow robot policies), yet DM1 is never included as a baseline in any of the quantitative comparisons (Tables 1, 2, 5), which is a significant omission given how directly comparable the stated problem framing is.

Reported performance gains over the strongest baseline (MP1) are modest on simulation benchmarks (82.3% vs 78.9% average, a ~3.4 point gain) and the evaluation protocol ('average of the five highest success-rates' checkpoints per run) is non-standard and could inflate absolute numbers / obscure true training stability relative to simpler max-at-convergence or last-checkpoint protocols.

Real-world results (Table 2) report point-estimate success rates over only 20 trials per task with no variance/confidence intervals, and training uses only 50 demonstrations per real task, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported 10-15% gains over MP1.

The preliminary experiments used to motivate 'spectral bias' and 'gradient starvation' (App C) rely on highly simplified synthetic setups (sum-of-sines MLP regression; a frozen-weight 2D vector gradient-descent toy problem) rather than direct diagnostic analysis on the actual manipulation policy networks/benchmarks, weakening the link between the theoretical motivation and the empirical method.

Simulation training uses only 10 demonstrations per task, an unusually low-data regime; combined with only 3 random seeds, the robustness of comparative conclusions versus baselines, especially for ablations showing single-digit percentage differences, is not strongly established.

strengths: Identifies three concrete and plausible failure modes of applying MeanFlow directly to robot policy learning (spectral bias, gradient starvation in low-velocity regimes, and memory complexity of nested JVP derivatives), each supported by a mathematical derivation plus a small controlled synthetic experiment (Fig. 2) that illustrates the phenomenon.

The proposed fix (Directional Alignment loss that decouples direction from magnitude via cosine similarity, Eq. 12) is simple, well-motivated by the gradient-starvation analysis, and easy to combine with the standard MSE/dispersive losses.

The DDE finite-difference approximation to the JVP is a practical, low-overhead way to reduce memory footprint, and Table 3 shows meaningful memory savings (e.g., ~7.5GB reduction on the larger 'Place Bottle' setting) that would matter when scaling to bigger backbones.

Evaluation breadth is good for the venue: 3 Adroit tasks + 34 Meta-World tasks across four difficulty tiers, 3 random seeds, an ablation study isolating each loss term, a sensitivity analysis over action-chunk horizons (Short/Medium/Long, Appendix E.1), and additional real-robot experiments on 3 manipulation tasks, which is more thorough than many policy-learning papers at this venue.

Reported gains over strong, recent baselines (MP1, FlowPolicy, DP3) are consistent across most task difficulty tiers and are especially large on the hardest categories (Meta-World Hard/Very Hard, real-world Slip Ring), which is where the paper's motivating failure mode (low-velocity precision tasks) should matter most, lending some internal coherence to the story.
Training-stability curves (Fig. 5) and standard deviations across seeds are reported, showing tighter variance than baselines such as FlowPolicy, which is a useful practical property for deployment.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivations are not fully rigorous and contain inconsistencies: Theorem B.1 analyzes u(t) as the average from 0 to t, while the main text (Eq. 5) defines the MeanFlow average over an arbitrary interval [r,t]; the special case r=0 used in the proof does not establish the claimed general 1/ω^2 decay for arbitrary intervals, and no proof is given for the general case actually used in training.

The spectral-bias and gradient-starvation analyses rely on continuous-time, idealized models (stationary stochastic processes, gradient flow in polar coordinates) that abstract away SGD stochasticity, network parameterization, and interaction with other loss terms; the synthetic 'sum of sines' and frozen-weight 2D toy experiments (Figs. 2, Appendix C/D) are illustrative but have unclear external validity to the high-dimensional, non-stationary trajectories of real manipulation policies.

The ablation in Table 1 shows that removing Directional Alignment alone only drops average success from 82.3% to 78.3% (and removing dispersive loss alone to 81.2%), a relatively modest effect given the paper's framing of gradient starvation as a 'fundamental' and 'critical' barrier; the claim that Directional Alignment is 'fundamental to the stability and high success rate of OMP' is somewhat stronger than the quantitative evidence supports.

Real-world results (Table 2) are based on only 20 trials per task with no reported variance/confidence intervals, making some reported differences (e.g., 70% vs 65% on Clean Table) of uncertain statistical significance; no seeds or repeated runs are mentioned for the real-robot evaluation, unlike the simulation experiments.

The DDE perturbation constant ε (Eq. 14) is introduced without any sensitivity analysis or guidance on selection, despite finite-difference approximations being sensitive to this hyperparameter (bias-variance/numerical precision trade-off); this is a reproducibility gap for a core efficiency component of the method.

Evaluation is restricted to Adroit/Meta-World simulation and a small set of 3 custom real-world tasks; there is no comparison on larger, more standardized manipulation benchmarks (e.g., RoboMimic, real multi-task suites) or against the broader set of very recent one-step/flow-based policies mentioned only in the related-work appendix, limiting evidence for the claim of 'establishing a new standard' for real-time generative control.

The memory-complexity analysis in Appendix B.3 relies on a simplifying assumption that tangent vectors have identical size to primal activations to derive a clean 2x factor; this is a rough theoretical approximation not independently validated against fine-grained empirical profiling beyond aggregate GPU memory numbers in Table 3, which bundle together all architecture components.
